{{Short description|Theorem in stochastic analysis}}
In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[stochastic analysis]] &mdash; '''Dynkin's formula''' is a theorem giving the [[expected value]] of any suitably [[Smoothness|smooth function]] applied to a [[Feller process]] at a [[stopping time]]. It may be seen as a stochastic generalization of the (second) [[fundamental theorem of calculus]]. It is named after the [[Russia]]n [[mathematician]] [[Eugene Dynkin]].

==Statement of the theorem==
Let <math>X</math> be a Feller process with [[infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] <math>A</math>.
For a point <math>x</math> in the state-space of <math>X</math>, let <math>\mathbf P^x</math> denote the law of <math>X</math> given initial datum <math>X_0=x</math>, and let <math>\mathbf E^x</math> denote expectation with respect to <math>\mathbf P^x</math>.
Then for any function <math>f</math> in the domain of <math>A</math>, and any [[stopping time]] <math>\tau</math> with <math>\mathbf E[\tau]<+\infty</math>, '''Dynkin's formula''' holds:<ref>Kallenberg (2021), Lemma 17.21, p383.</ref>
:<math>
\mathbf{E}^{x} [f(X_{\tau})] = f(x) + \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau} A f (X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right].
</math>

==Example: Itô diffusions==
Let <math>X</math> be the <math>\mathbf R^n</math>-valued [[Itô diffusion]] solving the [[stochastic differential equation]]

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_{t} = b(X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{t}.</math>

The infinitesimal generator <math>A</math> of <math>X</math> is defined by its action on [[compact support|compactly-supported]] <math>C^2</math> (twice differentiable with continuous [[second derivative]]) functions <math>f:\mathbf R^n \to \mathbf R</math> as<ref>Øksendal (2003), Definition 7.3.1, p124.</ref>

:<math>A f (x) = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathbf{E}^{x} [f(X_{t})] - f(x)}{t}</math>

or, equivalently,<ref>Øksendal (2003), Theorem 7.3.3, p126.</ref>

:<math>A f (x) = \sum_{i} b_{i} (x) \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} (x) + \frac1{2} \sum_{i, j} \big( \sigma \sigma^{\top} \big)_{i, j} (x) \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_{i}\, \partial x_{j}} (x).</math>

Since this <math>X</math> is a Feller process, Dynkin's formula holds.<ref name=oksendal>Øksendal (2003), Theorem 7.4.1, p127.</ref>
In fact, if <math>\tau</math> is the first exit time of a [[bounded set]] <math>B\subset\mathbf R^n</math> with <math>\mathbf E[\tau]<+\infty</math>, then Dynkin's formula holds for all <math>C^2</math> functions <math>f</math>, without the assumption of compact support.{{r|oksendal}}

==Application: Brownian motion exiting the ball==
Dynkin's formula can be used to find the expected first exit time <math>\tau_K</math> of a [[Brownian motion]] <math>B</math> from the [[closed ball]]
<math>K= \{ x \in \mathbf{R}^{n} : \, | x | \leq R \},</math>
which, when <math>B</math> starts at a point <math>a</math> in the [[interior (topology)|interior]] of <math>K</math>, is given by

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{a} [\tau_{K}] = \frac1{n} \big( R^{2} - | a |^{2} \big).</math>

This is shown as follows.<ref>Øksendal (2003), Example 7.4.2, p127.</ref> Fix an [[integer]] ''j''. The strategy is to apply Dynkin's formula with <math>X=B</math>, <math>\tau=\sigma_j=\min\{j,\tau_K\}</math>, and a compactly-supported <math>f\in C^2</math> with <math>f(x)=|x|^2</math> on <math>K</math>. The generator of Brownian motion is <math>\Delta/2</math>, where <math>\Delta</math> denotes the [[Laplacian operator]]. Therefore, by Dynkin's formula,

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{E}^{a} \left[ f \big( B_{\sigma_{j}} \big) \right]
&= f(a) + \mathbf{E}^{a} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sigma_{j}} \frac1{2} \Delta f (B_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right] \\
&= | a |^{2} + \mathbf{E}^{a} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sigma_{j}} n \, \mathrm{d} s \right]
= | a |^{2} + n \mathbf{E}^{a} [\sigma_{j}].
\end{align}</math>
Hence, for any <math>j</math>,

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{a} [\sigma_{j}] \leq \frac1{n} \big( R^{2} - | a |^{2} \big).</math>

Now let <math>j\to+\infty</math> to conclude that <math>\tau_K=\lim_{j\to+\infty}\sigma_j<+\infty</math> [[almost surely]], and so
<math>\mathbf{E}^{a} [\tau_{K}] =( R^{2} - | a |^{2})/n</math>
as claimed.
